one_liner: Header-only C++03 R-tree and 2D quadtree that compile about 25x faster than Boost.Geometry rtree code; runtime is not faster overall.
what_it_does: THST provides spatial::RTree<T, Value, Dim, M, m, Indexable, VolumeMode, RealType, Allocator> (N-dimensional, quadratic split) and spatial::QuadTree<T, Value, M, Indexable, Allocator> (2D, fixed world box) with near-identical interfaces. Queries take predicates (spatial::intersects/contains/within) and an output iterator, similar to Boost.Geometry's rtree, plus a ray-box query, a radius nearest query (2D only), an incremental k_nearest, conditional insert with a predicate, remove, translate, and leaf/depth-first iterators that expose internal ('hierarchical') nodes. It is not a drop-in for boost::geometry::index::rtree: the value type, indexable getter (min()/max() returning pointers) and query predicates are THST's own.
how_it_is_fast: The compile-time win comes from a small templated code base (Guttman's 1984 R-tree via the Greg Douglas / nushoin C++ ports) with none of Boost.Geometry's concept, variant-visitor and strategy machinery. At runtime it uses Guttman's quadratic split (pickSeeds/classify) with an optional spherical-volume measure, fixed-size nodes holding parallel arrays of values, boxes and child pointers, and a pluggable node allocator; the benchmark's fastest THST variant uses a test-only allocator that places all nodes in one pre-sized std::vector. There is no bulk loading (listed under 'Future improvements'), no R*-tree reinsertion and no SIMD.
when_to_use: Projects where build time matters and Boost.Geometry's rtree headers dominate compile time: the README reports 1.4 s vs 35.3 s to compile the benchmark program
Games, physics and editors that rebuild or heavily update a small index every frame: the project's dynamic benchmark shows THST quadratic ahead of bgi linear above about 400 objects

Hierarchical scene partitioning where you want to store data on internal nodes, walk the tree level by level (dbegin/child iterators) or stop a query once a node is fully contained (hierachical_query)
Ray casting against boxes (rayQuery with a filter predicate) without pulling in a BVH library
Old toolchains: the core RTree/QuadTree is written for C++03 and needs no dependencies
when_not_to_use: Query-heavy static data: per the project's own charts, Boost.Geometry rtree with bulk loading or R* gives the best query times, ahead of THST's best (quadratic with custom allocator)
Large static datasets that you can bulk-load: THST has only one-by-one insertion, while Boost's packing algorithm loads fastest
Fewer than about 400 objects in a rebuild-every-frame loop: bgi linear was slightly faster there in the same benchmark
QuadTree for 1M-box workloads: the benchmark README calls quadtree queries 'really slow' and building 'very slow' for capacities 256-1024
Code that needs active maintenance or a package: last commit March 2024, issue #23 (assertion failure in RTree::choosePartition, Oct 2023) is still open, and there is no vcpkg port (issue #26 open)

integration.dependencies: none (the benchmark needs Boost headers, CMake and gnuplot; tests use doctest as a git submodule)
integration.min_toolchain: C++03 for the core trees; RTree::k_nearest (priority_queue::emplace) and QuadTree::clear (nullptr) need C++11; move constructors are enabled under C++11/MSVC 2013+
integration.platforms: any (portable scalar C++; benchmarked on macOS with Xcode, CMake files also handle MSVC, GCC and Clang)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; from the source, queries are const and use only local state, while insert/remove modify a shared member scratch buffer (m_parVars), so writes need external locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the query style (predicate + output iterator) and indexable getter resemble Boost.Geometry's rtree, but the template parameters, predicate names and getter signature differ, and there is no bulk loading, R*/linear split or general nearest() predicate

gotchas: Several failure cases are checked only by assert, so release builds do not catch them: inserting a box outside a QuadTree's world box, more than 16 levels in the depth/leaf iterators' fixed stack (a write past the array), and the under-filled node split reported in open issue #23
RTree::nearest(point, radius) is 2D only (static assert) and ranks by distance to box centre; k_nearest works in N dimensions and uses minimum distance to the box
Node capacity and min fill are template parameters (defaults M=8, m=M/2); the benchmark sweeps M from small values up to 40x the base and results depend strongly on it
The 'custom' allocator in the benchmark is test/custom_allocator.h, not part of include/; it must be pre-sized (nodeCount * 1.5) and only asserts on overflow
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick THST over tidwall/rtree.c or GeoToolbox KdBoxTree when you want a templated, header-only C++ tree with hierarchical iteration, ray queries and low compile cost; pick those siblings (or nanoflann for point k-NN) when raw insert/query throughput against Boost is the goal, since THST's own benchmark does not show a runtime win over a bulk-loaded Boost rtree.
verified_claims_summary: The author reused Loskot and Wulkiewicz's spatial_index_benchmark: 1M small random boxes inserted iteratively, 100K intersection queries with boxes 10x larger, and a 200-run dynamic clear/query/insert loop, comparing THST quadtree/quadratic/quadratic-sphere (heap and custom allocator) with Boost.Geometry rtree linear/quadratic/R* (iterative and bulk, compile-time parameters) on an Intel Core i7-4870HQ under macOS Sierra, built as an Xcode Release (exact compiler and flags not stated). The only numeric claim is benchmark compile time, 35.3 s for Boost vs 1.4 s for THST; runtime results are PNG charts in which Boost bulk/R* leads queries and THST quadratic wins only the dynamic case above about 400 objects.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2024-03-16, a CMake install-script PR) but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small (RTree.h is about 1,800 lines, QuadTree.h about 800), so easy to vendor; treat it as a compile-time and feature pick, not a runtime-speed pick.
